title: Nell's Quiet Day Emergency
markdown:
The valley sat cupped between mountains that slept with snow on their heads even in warm weeks. On a rocky ledge lived Witch Nell, cottage a cheerful argument of drying herbs and pots, cinnamon and rain. Marmalade, amber-eyed, orange as his name, purred like thought and noticed everything.

Nell did not do loud magic. She liked tea, a charm that fitted a problem exactly, and days whose largest drama was a knot. She had hung a sign: Quiet Day. Please watch from afar if you must watch. She meant it.

“Patience,” she told the chamomile pot. “We shall just be. Sewing, perhaps.” Marmalade, a furry puddle on the sill, blinked. His purr shook the timbers in a civilised way.

Quiet rarely keeps the appointment. Nell had threaded a needle, set it down, and watched the steam choose a lazy spiral. Marmalade’s ear ticked at a sound that was not yet a knock. A day’s walk off, at the Sunstone Peaks, young Elara had brewed a mix that taught flowers to sing—lovely at a concert, alarming in prize moon-petunias, who were now performing sad arias to a moon that was not even on duty. Neighbours had begun to close shutters. Buttercups, rumour said, were taking it personally. The fix was Nell’s Quietude Quencher, a brew that reminded plants about volume and people about sleep. She had bottled the last batch in spring and hoped not to need it until she was bored.

Taps, sharp, on the door. Quillan the Goat, horns wiggling, heart full of good ideas and a calendar full of bad timing. “The petunias are singing at the top of their leafy lungs. Emergency of the loudest kind.”

“I am having a quiet day. The sign is clear.”

“They’re out of tune. The buttercups are drooping.”

A messenger arrived before diplomacy could put its boots on, side clutched, a stoppered vial glowing soft green pressed into Nell’s hand. “No time. Sunset. Heartbreaking.” He left the potion and the ruin of her schedule.

“Quiet has taken a corner,” Nell told Marmalade, tucking the vial into the apron pocket built for delicate glass. He hopped down, understanding in amber.

Quillan loved a journey the way some people love a drum. “I’ll come. I prevent losing. And snack-forgetting.”

She could have pointed at the sign. The distant floral misery made him useful; he knew the paths. “Quietly. No volunteering unless asked.”

He trotted, a whirlwind of commentary: loose stone, view, clouds that were sheep and required names. Then the bridge: slim, old dark wood over a green gorge, planks polished by years of other people’s hurry. Nell checked each board. Marmalade crossed as if silence were a skill.

Quillan stopped. “Shaky. Shortcut through the Whispering Woods. The wind mentioned clover.”

“I anti-wobbled it last spring.” She showed a thumb-sized tool that glittered with stubbornness. “Steady.”

He was already on the overgrown path, interesting and better views. Nell sighed dandelion-soft. Marmalade mrrrowed. The vial, the sinking sun, orange and purple. “The long way, then.”

The Whispering Woods whispered, as advertised, mostly about clover and once about a shortcut that was a lie. Prickles took her cloak in several small taxes. Squirrels complained in a dialect Marmalade refused to translate. A bog made boots confess; Nell dried them with a mutter that smelled briefly of toast. She untangled, calmed, stitched the day with spells too small to boast about. Quillan declared every weed a picnic, named a cloud Gerald, and did not notice the stitches. The vial ticked against a button like a second, more useful heart. The sun leaned west as if it, too, had a festival to ruin.

They came out on a ledge too far down, Peaks a dark shape, time running like water through a cup. Marmalade sniffed, detective-serious, trotted to the edge, meowed at the highest point, nudged her hand. A watcher’s lamp flickered in twilight, nearer from here than the proper road had promised.

“You took the very long way,” Nell said, tiredness briefly unemployed, “and it was also, inconveniently, the direct one.”

They climbed. Scramble, not stroll. Quillan, sorry at last, nudged loose stones aside with a useful head. Marmalade placed her feet with purrs. They reached the courtyard as the last sun went. Worried faces. A chorus of beautiful heartbroken plants. Nell held out the vial, voice calm above the floral weather.

Elara, face wet with the particular tears of almost-ruined prizes, dosed the loudest moon-petunias first. Songs became sighs, then leaves remembering their job. A hush moved the courtyard the way a good charm moves a room. Thanks arrived as tea that smelled of sunstone and honey cake that did not sing, quiet joy, the kind that does not need a speech. Steam misted a window; rain began on the sill as if the mountain had also wanted a quieter volume. It was not the sewing day. It was, Nell allowed, a day that had earned its armchair, and Elara’s whispered sorry, which Nell waved off as one brewer to another.

Home under a half-moon that had the decency not to sing, Quillan unusually short of names for clouds, Marmalade a warm weight on her shoulder. Once the goat started to describe a rock and thought better of it. The cottage smelled of lavender and the sign still hung, slightly askew from enthusiasm. She straightened it a finger’s width and left the rest. She sat in the chair that knew her. Marmalade found her lap as if laps were a science. The embroidery waited, knot and all. Tea, this time, stayed tea. Quiet, when it finally came, had walked a long shortcut to get there, and Nell, who liked things to fit, allowed that this one fitted well enough.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
